extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, journalists, policymakers, and anyone studying propaganda/press influences
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and dimensions for understanding how information, censorship, media practices, and social conditions shape public opinion and the appearance of news. Useful for evaluating press output, propaganda, and mechanisms that produce collective beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of reality (pseudo-environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him ... The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if an atlas tells a man the world is flat he will avoid the edge; if maps show a fountain of youth explorers will pursue it. The text emphasizes that communications create 'pseudo-environments'—interior representations that determine effort, feelings, and hopes though not necessarily actual results. Propaganda and class or national consciousness are processes of substituting one social pattern (picture) for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barrier/controlled access required for propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible. In order to conduct a propaganda there must be some barrier between the public and the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barriers include military censorship, control of cables, passports, mails, custom houses, blockades, legal powers over publishers and meetings, and secret services. When access to the real environment is limited, an organized group can decide what the public will see and therefore shape the 'pseudo-environment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and framing of facts to shape public reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of men, who can prevent independent access to the event, arrange the news of it to suit their purpose ... They used their power to make the Allied publics see affairs as they desired them to be seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by French wartime communiqués: careful choice of nouns, adjectives, and verbs (e.g., inserting reassuring phrases, omitting damaging details) to steady morale. Framing may omit one's own losses, emphasize enemy casualties, or craft narratives that guide inferences without explicit argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and statistical framing to manufacture impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant repetition impressed the neutrals and Germany itself, and helped to create a bloody background ... Every fortnight the figures increased a hundred thousand or so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of repeated casualty statistics and catch-phrases (e.g., 'mowed down by our artillery') produces a striking effect that shapes belief. Repetition, routine formulae, and statistical inflation can create and sustain particular interpretations in publics and among neutrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of journalists/correspondents and message flows
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Staff of an army in the field is so placed that within wide limits it can control what the public will perceive. It controls the selection of correspondents who go to the front, controls their movements at the front, reads and censors their messages from the front, and operates the wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: choosing who may report, supervising their access and movement, censoring telegrams/dispatches, and managing transmission channels. This operational control is a primary means by which authorities shape reports reaching the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and leaks that constrain censorship effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: But in the case of an army the control is far from perfect. There is always the enemy's communique, which in these days of wireless cannot be kept away from neutrals. Above all there is the talk of the soldiers, which blows back from the front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with tight censorship, rival reports, wireless transmissions, soldier talk, and other informal channels can undermine official narratives. Evaluators should consider such independent or adversarial information flows when judging the reliability or completeness of official press output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and chain-of-reporting (who actually saw/heard/felt)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often very illuminating ... to ask yourself how you got at the facts on which you base your opinion. Who actually saw, heard, felt, counted, named the thing, about which you have an opinion? Was it the man who told you, or the man who told him, or someone still further removed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess distance from original event, permitted access of the observer, what parts of a population were observed, and where reporters drew their information. This check on sources is a protection against accepting a distorted pseudo-environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms of privacy and evolving boundaries of publishable information
rubrics_metrics.description: At different times and for different subjects some men impose and other men accept a particular standard of secrecy ... The notion of what constitutes a person's private affairs is elastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: incomes, salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet meetings, and medical or theological matters have been treated variously as private or public across history. Assessments of media transparency should account for socially accepted privacy and how it limits information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution capacity and resource intensity to reach publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Probably this is the largest and the most intensive effort to carry quickly a fairly uniform set of ideas to all the people of a nation ... Mr. Creel had to assemble machinery which included a Division of News that issued ... more than six thousand releases ... 75,000 Four Minute Men ... posters, newspaper advertisements, cartoons, seals and buttons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaching 'everybody' requires complex organizations, personnel, money, and logistical channels. In peacetime such machinery rarely exists, so many groups or enclaves hear only vaguely about broader affairs. When evaluating claims of mass reach, consider the scale and costs of distribution employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/infrastructural barriers to circulation (monopoly, cost, access)
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopolizing of cables ... ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, market places means a good deal more than the enrichment of a group of business men ... It means a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopoly control of communication/transport nodes and economic factors like tariffs, subsidies, and costs create practical barriers to the flow of ideas. Evaluate who controls key infrastructure and how that shapes which messages spread and which are suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, attention, and compression constraints on message clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: the comparatively meager time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs, the distortion arising because events have to be compressed into very short messages, the difficulty of making a small vocabulary express a complicated world
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short attention spans and tight formats force compression and simplification, increasing risk of distortion. Assess whether communicators have compressed complex events into oversimple narratives or jargon-limited reports that mislead through omission or simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceptions, stereotypes, and stored images shaping interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: the stored up images, the preconceptions, and prejudices which interpret, fill them out, and in their turn powerfully direct the play of our attention, and our vision itself ... formed into a pattern of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People interpret incoming messages through existing stock images and stereotypes; communicators exploit or encounter these when crafting narratives. Evaluation should examine how messages fit into or alter prevailing stereotypes and whether they are being 'filled out' by audience biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert organization to represent unseen facts to decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government ... cannot be worked successfully ... unless there is an independent, expert organization for making the unseen facts intelligible to those who have to make the decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press cannot be expected to supply comprehensive, accurate representations of complex unseen realities at no cost. Policy and democratic functioning require specialized, independent organizations (e.g., political science/formal analysis bodies) to synthesize and present facts prior to decision-making.
